description: MATA: Tanaw (Mapping A Typhoon Aftermath: Tracking Affected Neighborhoods Across Waters) is a SAR-based decision-support web app. Using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 backscatter change detection, it replays how typhoon floods spread and receded in Philippine river basins and maps how long each barangay stayed underwater, with uncertainty ranges. Exposure indices and resident photo validation help LGUs and DRRM offices prioritize drainage, evacuation, and recovery.
summary: MATA: TANAW is a SAR-based decision-support web app. Using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 backscatter change detection, it replays how typhoon floods spread and receded in Laguna Bay and maps how long each barangay stayed underwater, with uncertainty ranges. Exposure indices provided by the app help Locals, LGUs, and DRRM offices crowdsource which areas must be prioritized for drainage systems, evacuation, and recovery.
details:
When a typhoon hits Laguna de Bay, the clouds that come with it block the optical satellites that most flood maps rely on. MATA: Tanaw gets around this with SAR. Tanaw is Tagalog for looking out over something from a distance, and the web app does this for the lakeshore barangays of Santa Cruz, Pila, Victoria, and Bay. Radar can see through cloud and works day or night, so the app can show where floodwater spread and how it receded while the storm was still overhead.

The app starts with Sentinel-1 radar scenes, where open water shows up as dark patches, and uses them to build a replay of flooding from 2024 to 2026. One radar image can be misleading, so we check it against other sources. NASA’s OPERA surface-water product flags open water and flooded vegetation. NISAR’s L-band radar penetrates crops and tree canopy better than Sentinel-1 does. InSAR coherence, which measures how much the radar signal changes between passes, gives hints of flooding in dense town centers, where water between buildings is hard to see. We then clean the results using elevation data to remove the slopes toward Mount Makiling and the radar shadows they cause. Land-cover data helps us separate the lake, fishpens, and built-up areas from land that was newly flooded.

The cleaned flood layers are laid over official barangay boundaries and OpenStreetMap buildings, on top of a cloud-free satellite basemap. We also add DAHITI satellite measurements of the lake’s water level. That helps users tell whether a flood came from rivers overflowing after heavy rain or from the lake itself rising and pushing water back onto the shore.

This is useful for several reasons. Radar works through storm cloud, and combining several kinds of radar catches flooding in places a single sensor would miss, such as rice fields, marshes, and the poblacion of Santa Cruz. Because everything is tied to barangay boundaries and building footprints, officials and residents see what happened in their own village instead of a broad provincial estimate. Putting past floods next to the lake-level record also gives communities a way to learn from patterns across years.

With these benefits, we hope to make satellite radar data usable by the people who need it most. Municipal and barangay disaster risk reduction offices could use the app to find hard-hit lowland and lakeshore barangays during a typhoon and direct rescue, evacuation, and relief to them. Planners could use the multi-year record, together with the lake-level trends, to make decisions about zoning, farmland protection, and drainage. The app also turns raw NASA and Copernicus data, which normally takes specialist software to read, into a map that anyone can open in a browser.

To build it, we used React 19, JavaScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS 4 for the web app, with MapLibre GL JS, Three.js, and PMTiles for the 2D and 3D maps. The data processing was done in Python with NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, Pyogrio, Pillow, and h5py. We pulled Sentinel-1 scenes from Microsoft Planetary Computer, ran InSAR and NISAR processing through the Alaska Satellite Facility’s HyP3 service, and downloaded OPERA data from NASA’s PO.DAAC. Elevation and land-cover data came from AWS Open Data, and the basemap uses OpenStreetMap through Protomaps and OpenFreeMap. All the heavy radar processing ran in the cloud, so ordinary laptops were enough.

Our four-radar approach, rather than relying on one thresholded image, allows for other factors to cover a weakness of the others, and the mix matches the land around the lake: a dense town, flat farmland, and vegetated shoreline. We also kept the interface honest. It labels main flood observations separately from supporting evidence, marks NISAR data that is still provisional, and says which map elements are only for context or decoration. We wanted people to see this as a tool for decisions, not as perfect ground truth.

Since the four towns sit on low, flat plains where floods can come from both river overflow and lake rise, while the southern part of Bay climbs steeply toward Mount Makiling, we used elevation and land-cover masks to keep mountain shadows and permanent water from being mistaken for flood. We knew that standard radar can miss water under trees, crops, or between buildings, which is why we brought in NISAR and InSAR and flagged the provisional NISAR products that may be reprocessed, and kept analytical flood layers visually separate from decorative ones so no one reads a background feature as live flood data.
